name: Concurrency and Async
author: Recurse
subject: swe
description: Threads, processes, races, locks and deadlock, the JavaScript event loop, async/await, asyncio, the GIL and thread pools.

lesson.intro: Concurrency bugs pass every test, then corrupt data at 2 a.m. under real load. This lesson builds the mental models: threads and processes, lost updates, locks and deadlocks, the JavaScript event loop, and when to use threads, asyncio or processes in Python.
objectives: Tell processes from threads, and concurrency from parallelism
Explain a race condition and fix it with a lock or an atomic operation
Name the four deadlock conditions and prevent deadlock with a lock order
Predict the output of code mixing synchronous code, promises and setTimeout
Choose between async/await, threads, processes and pools for a task

sections.title: Processes, threads, concurrency and parallelism
sections.key: Concurrency interleaves tasks over the same period; parallelism runs them at the same instant on different cores. I/O-bound work gains from the first, CPU-bound only from the second.
sections.body:
Hundreds of processes and thousands of threads share maybe 8 cores, yet music plays while code compiles.

[[visual]]

Interviewers want two words kept apart. **Concurrency** is structure: several tasks in progress at once, their steps interleaved, like one cook keeping three pans going. **Parallelism** is execution: tasks running at the same instant on different cores, like three cooks.

[[visual 2]]

[[visual 3]]

A single-threaded Node.js server is highly concurrent and not parallel at all. Most work is one of two kinds:

[[visual 4]]

items.title: Process
points: A running program with its own private memory: variables, heap, open files
Isolated: one crashed browser tab leaves the others alone
Talks through pipes, sockets and files

items.title: Thread
points: A path of execution inside a process
Shares the process's memory with its siblings: power and danger

visual.title: One core: concurrency
visual.caption: All three tasks progress, one at a time (time slicing).

items.title: I/O-bound
points: Mostly waiting on networks, disks or databases
Concurrency helps a lot, even on one core: while one task waits, another runs

items.title: CPU-bound
points: Keeps a core busy: resizing images, compression, number crunching
Only parallelism across cores makes it faster

sections.tip: When someone says "make it faster with threads", ask first: is it waiting on I/O or burning CPU? The answer decides the tool.
sections.pitfall: Using "concurrent" and "parallel" as synonyms. A single-threaded Node.js server is highly concurrent and not parallel at all.

activity.title: Concurrency on one CPU
activity.prompt: Run the same processes under first-come first-served and round robin. Round robin is concurrency on a single CPU: no two processes ever run at the same instant, yet every process starts making progress early. Watch the Gantt chart interleave, then compare the average waiting times.

check.question: A single-core machine runs a web server that keeps 500 connections open, switching between them while each waits on the database. What is this?
choices: Parallelism, because 500 requests are in progress
Concurrency without parallelism
Neither concurrency nor parallelism
Parallelism, because time slicing counts as parallel
check.explanation: Many tasks are in progress and interleave, which is concurrency. With one core, nothing runs at the same instant, so there is no parallelism.

sections.title: Race conditions: the lost increment
sections.key: `counter += 1` is a read, an add and a write; if another thread runs between the read and the write, an update is lost. That is a race condition.
sections.body:
Four threads each add 1,000 to a shared page-view counter. You expect 4,000 and get 1,004. `counter += 1` is really three steps: **read**, **add**, **write**. If a thread pauses between its read and its write while another runs, an update is lost:

[[visual]]

That is a **race condition**: the result depends on thread timing. Code that touches shared state and must not interleave is a **critical section**.

The example widens the gap with `time.sleep(0)` so the bug shows every run. With a plain `counter += 1` the gap is tiny and the bug is rare, which is worse: it passes tests and appears under production load.

[[code]]

The same read-then-act shape appears everywhere:

[[visual 2]]

visual.title: One lost update, counter starts at 41

messages.note: B never saw A's write: two increments, one lost

visual.title: Race shapes
rows: both read the old value, one write is lost
two withdrawals pass the check before either subtracts; the balance goes negative
A database row in app code
read a row, change it, write it back
the lost update from the databases lesson
visual.caption: The cure: make the read and the write one indivisible unit, with a lock or an atomic operation.

sections.code:
import threading, time

counter = 0

def work():
    global counter
    for _ in range(1000):
        current = counter    # 1. read
        time.sleep(0)        # others run
        counter = current + 1  # 2. write

threads = [threading.Thread(target=work)
           for _ in range(4)]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()
print(counter)  # not 4000: about 1004
sections.deeper: Recent CPython versions switch threads less often in the middle of a tight loop, so a plain `counter += 1` race may look correct on your machine for a long time. It is still a race: a busier machine, a different Python version or the free-threaded build can expose it. The only proof of safety is synchronization, never a passing test run.
sections.tip: If two threads can touch the same variable and at least one of them writes it, you need synchronization. No exceptions for "it's just a counter".
sections.pitfall: Concluding there is no race because the tests pass. Races depend on timing, so they hide on an idle laptop and appear under load.

check.question: Two threads each run `counter += 1` once. How can counter end up increased by only 1?
choices: Python rounds integers that are shared between threads
Threads are not allowed to write to global variables
The operation is a separate read, add and write, and both threads can read the old value before either writes
join() undoes one of the two writes
check.explanation: Both threads read the same old value, both add 1, and both write the same result, so one increment disappears. The fix is to make read, add and write one indivisible step.

sections.title: Locks and atomic operations
sections.key: A lock lets only one thread at a time run the critical section; an atomic operation such as compare-and-swap updates a single value safely without one.
sections.body:
A **lock** (or **mutex**, for mutual exclusion) enforces one thread at a time: **acquire** it before the critical section, **release** it after, and any other thread trying to acquire it waits. In Python, `with lock:` guarantees release even if an exception is raised.

[[code]]

[[visual]]

An **atomic operation** completes as one indivisible step. The CPU's **compare-and-swap** (CAS) is the building block:

[[visual 2]]

Languages expose atomics: Java's `AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet()`, Go's `sync/atomic`, JavaScript's `Atomics.add`. Each covers one variable; two related values still need a lock or a transaction. Python has no atomic integer, so use a `Lock`, give each thread its own result, or pass work through `queue.Queue`.

visual.title: Using locks well
rows: one unguarded read can see a half-finished update
a lock created inside the function is new on every call and protects nothing
never hold a lock during a network call, query or sleep: every other thread waits
one big lock is simple but serializes threads; a lock per account allows more parallelism but risks deadlock
`acquire()` without `release()` in a `finally` leaves the lock held forever after one exception

steps.label: CAS: set it to 43 only if it still holds 42
steps.no: Someone changed it: read again and retry

sections.code:
import threading

counter = 0
lock = threading.Lock()  # one, shared

def work():
    global counter
    for _ in range(100_000):
        with lock:  # released even on error
            counter += 1
# 4 threads of work() always give 400000
sections.deeper: When the shared state lives in a database, let the database be atomic for you: `UPDATE counters SET n = n + 1 WHERE id = 1` is one atomic statement, while reading the row into Python, adding 1 and writing it back is the same lost-update race as the threaded counter. The safest shared state is none at all: give each worker its own data and merge the results at the end.
sections.tip: The safest shared state is no shared state. Prefer giving each worker its own data and merging results, or passing messages through a queue.
sections.pitfall: Holding a lock while making a network call or a database query. Every other thread stalls behind one slow request.

check.question: What does a compare-and-swap (CAS) instruction do?
choices: Swaps the values of two variables while holding a lock
Atomically sets a value only if it still equals an expected value, and reports whether it succeeded
Compares two threads and pauses the slower one
Copies a shared variable into each thread's private memory
check.explanation: CAS is the building block of lock-free code: read the value, compute the new one, and swap it in only if nobody changed it meanwhile. If the swap fails, read again and retry.

sections.title: Deadlock and its four conditions
sections.key: Deadlock needs all four Coffman conditions at once; break any one and it cannot happen. A single global lock order, which breaks circular wait, is the first fix.
sections.body:
A banking service locks both accounts during each transfer. It runs for weeks, then two requests hang forever:

[[visual]]

That is a **deadlock**. It can happen only when all four **Coffman conditions** hold:

[[visual 2]]

[[code]]

Databases face the same issue with row locks: they detect the cycle and abort one transaction with a deadlock error, which your code should catch and retry.

Related terms: **livelock**, where threads keep reacting to each other and retrying without progress, and **starvation**, where one thread never wins the resource.

messages.note: Thread 1 moves A to B; Thread 2 moves B to A
Each holds what the other needs: neither can ever continue

rows: Mutual exclusion: one holder at a time (a lock)
fewer locks, or no shared state
Hold and wait: holds one, waits for another
all or nothing: take every lock, or release and retry
No preemption: nobody can take it away
timeouts: `lock.acquire(timeout=1)`, then release and retry with random backoff
Circular wait: a cycle of waiting threads
**lock ordering**: for example, always lock the smaller account id first

sections.code:
# Deadlock-prone: order depends on direction
def transfer(src, dst, amount):
    with src.lock:
        with dst.lock:
            src.balance -= amount
            dst.balance += amount

# Fixed: one global order, smaller id first
def transfer(src, dst, amount):
    first, second = sorted(
        [src, dst], key=lambda a: a.id)
    with first.lock:
        with second.lock:
            src.balance -= amount
            dst.balance += amount
sections.tip: When you see nested locks in a code review, ask "is the order the same everywhere?" That one question prevents most deadlocks.
sections.pitfall: "Fixing" a deadlock with sleeps or retries without breaking one of the four conditions. The hang becomes rarer and much harder to reproduce.

check.question: Which change prevents the transfer deadlock by breaking the circular-wait condition?
choices: Adding time.sleep(0.1) between the two lock acquisitions
Running the transfers on more threads
Logging every lock acquisition
Always locking the two accounts in a fixed order, such as smaller id first
check.explanation: If every thread takes locks in the same global order, no cycle of waiting threads can form. Sleeps and logging only change the timing, so the deadlock becomes rarer but still possible.

sections.title: The JavaScript event loop
sections.key: The event loop runs the script to completion, then every microtask (promise callbacks), then one task (such as a setTimeout callback), draining microtasks again after each task.
sections.body:
JavaScript runs your code on one thread, yet Node.js serves thousands of connections. The **call stack** runs synchronous code; slow work (timers, network, files) is handed to the browser or Node, and its callback is queued when it completes. There are two queues:

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

So promise callbacks always run before the next `setTimeout` callback, even one with a 0 ms delay. `setTimeout(fn, 0)` means "as a new task, after the script and every pending microtask", not "now".

[[code]]

[[visual 3]]

One thread also means a long synchronous loop **blocks the event loop**: no timers fire, no requests are answered, the page cannot repaint. Move heavy work to a Web Worker or worker thread, or split it into chunks.

visual.title: The loop's rule

steps.label: Run the script until the call stack is empty
Run every microtask
steps.detail: including microtasks queued by other microtasks, until the queue is empty

steps.label: Take one task from the task queue and run it

visual.loop: Back to the microtasks after every task

steps.label: Synchronous code prints, then the stack is empty
The first .then prints 3, queues task 4 and the next .then
Now tasks, one at a time, in queue order

sections.code:
console.log('1')

setTimeout(() => console.log('2'), 0)

Promise.resolve()
  .then(() => {
    console.log('3')
    setTimeout(() => console.log('4'), 0)
  })
  .then(() => console.log('5'))

queueMicrotask(() => console.log('6'))

console.log('7')
sections.tip: For any ordering puzzle, keep three columns on paper: synchronous output, microtask queue, task queue. Fill them as you read, then drain them in that order.
sections.pitfall: Believing `setTimeout(fn, 0)` runs immediately, or before promise callbacks. It waits for the current script and every queued microtask.

activity.title: Predict the order
activity.prompt: Before you run it, write down the order of the six lines. Notice that the Promise executor (C) runs synchronously. Then move the queueMicrotask line above the Promise and predict again: which lines change places, and which never can?

props.code:
console.log('A: script start')

setTimeout(() => console.log('B: timeout'), 0)

new Promise((resolve) => {
  console.log('C: executor runs right away')
  resolve()
}).then(() => console.log('D: then'))

queueMicrotask(() => console.log('E: microtask'))

console.log('F: script end')

props.expectOutput:
A: script start
C: executor runs right away
F: script end

check.question: The current script finishes. A `setTimeout(fn, 0)` callback was queued before a `.then` callback. Which runs first?
choices: The setTimeout callback, because it was queued first
The .then callback, because every microtask runs before the next task
Both at once, on different threads
It is random and differs between runs
check.explanation: Promise callbacks are microtasks, and the loop drains all microtasks before taking the next task from the task queue. Queue order only matters within the same queue.

sections.title: async/await in JavaScript
sections.key: An async function runs synchronously until its first await, then resumes later as a microtask; start independent calls together and await them with Promise.all.
sections.body:
A dashboard loads three endpoints of about 300 ms each and takes 900 ms. A small change makes it 300 ms. `async`/`await` is syntax on promises:

- An `async` function always returns a promise.
- `await` pauses that function, not the program; the rest resumes as a microtask when the promise settles.
- An async function runs synchronously until its first `await`, so below, `B` prints before `C`.

[[code]]

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

[[visual 3]]

visual.title: Three independent 300 ms calls
visual.caption: Concurrent calls take about as long as the slowest one, not the sum.

visual.title: Combinators
rows: every result in order, or rejects as soon as any rejects (the others keep running, ignored)
`{ status, value }` or `{ status, reason }` for each: use when partial results are fine
whichever settles first, handy for timeouts

visual.title: Classic mistakes
rows: forEach ignores the promises, so nothing waits and failures go unhandled; use `for...of` with `await`, or `Promise.all` over `map` (see the code)
Awaiting independent calls one by one in a loop
each waits for the last: start them all, then await `Promise.all`
`getUser()` is a pending promise, so `user.name` is undefined
fires 10,000 requests at once: batch them or use a concurrency limiter

sections.tip: Before writing two awaits in a row, ask: does the second call need the first one's result? If not, start both and await them together.
sections.pitfall: Calling `forEach` with an async callback and expecting it to wait. It fires every callback and moves on immediately.

activity.title: Sequential versus concurrent
activity.prompt: Run it and compare the two timings. Then add a fourth 300 ms call to both functions and predict both new timings before you run it again. The sequential time grows with every call; the concurrent time tracks the slowest call.

props.task: Compare the two timings, then add a fourth call to each.

check.question: Three independent API calls take about 300 ms each. Roughly how long does `await Promise.all([a(), b(), c()])` take?
choices: About 100 ms
About 900 ms
About 300 ms
About 1,200 ms
check.explanation: All three requests are in flight at the same time, so the total is about as long as the slowest one, not the sum. Awaiting them one by one would take about 900 ms.

sections.title: asyncio in Python
sections.key: asyncio runs coroutines on one thread's event loop: await hands control back so others can run, and any blocking call inside async code freezes them all.
sections.body:
A script checks 200 URLs one after another at half a second each: almost two minutes, nearly all of it waiting. Python's tool for I/O-bound work is `asyncio`, the same event-loop idea as JavaScript:

[[visual]]

[[code]]

**Never block the event loop.** One thread runs every coroutine, so `time.sleep(1)`, `requests.get(...)` or a heavy loop inside `async def` freezes them all:

[[visual 2]]

Limit concurrency against real services too: an `asyncio.Semaphore(20)` lets only 20 requests run at a time. asyncio suits API fan-out, websockets, chat servers and scrapers, not CPU-bound work.

rows: defines a **coroutine function**; calling it only creates a coroutine object, which must be awaited or scheduled
pauses this coroutine and hands control to the event loop, which runs others
starts the loop, runs `main`, closes the loop; call it once, at the top
runs coroutines concurrently and returns results in order
starts one in the background right away
waits without blocking: the loop runs other coroutines meanwhile

sections.code:
import asyncio, time

async def check(url):
    await asyncio.sleep(1)  # the network
    return f"{url}: ok"

async def main():
    start = time.perf_counter()
    results = await asyncio.gather(
        check("a"), check("b"), check("c"))
    took = time.perf_counter() - start
    print(results, f"{took:.1f}s")  # 1.0s

asyncio.run(main())
# time.sleep(1) in check() would freeze
# the loop: about 3 seconds instead
sections.tip: An async function that calls a library without async support is probably blocking the loop. Look for requests, time.sleep and heavy loops.
sections.pitfall: Calling a coroutine function without await, as in `check(url)`. Nothing runs: Python creates a coroutine object and warns that it was never awaited.

check.question: Inside an `async def`, a teammate uses `time.sleep(2)` to wait between retries. What is the effect?
choices: Only that coroutine pauses, and the others keep running
Python quietly converts it to asyncio.sleep
It raises a SyntaxError inside async functions
The whole event loop freezes for 2 seconds, so every other coroutine waits too
check.explanation: time.sleep blocks the thread, and that one thread is running the event loop. Use await asyncio.sleep(2), which pauses only this coroutine and lets the loop run others.

sections.title: The GIL, multiprocessing and thread pools
sections.key: CPython's GIL lets one thread run Python bytecode at a time, so threads speed up I/O-bound work but not CPU-bound work, which needs processes.
sections.body:
Eight threads make an image resizer no faster on 8 cores, yet make a 200-file downloader about 8 times faster. The reason is CPython's **Global Interpreter Lock (GIL)**: in one process, only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time. A thread waiting on a socket, file or sleep releases it.

[[visual]]

The GIL does **not** make your code thread-safe: it protects the interpreter, not your read-modify-write steps. Python 3.13 added an opt-in **free-threaded** build without it, which still needs locks.

A **pool** keeps a fixed number of workers fed from a queue, instead of one thread per task:

[[visual 2]]

[[code]]

visual.title: Pick the tool
rows: each process has its own interpreter and GIL; costs: slower start, data pickled and copied
NumPy on big arrays, hashing, compression
these release the GIL while they run in C

visual.title: Pools in practice
rows: runs fn on every item, yields results in input order
returns a **Future**; `as_completed(futures)` yields them as they finish, and `future.result()` re-raises the task's error
waits for all work to finish
more than the cores (say 20 to 50), capped by what the remote service allows

sections.code:
from concurrent.futures import (
    ThreadPoolExecutor, ProcessPoolExecutor)

def main():
    # I/O-bound: threads, results in order
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(16) as pool:
        for url, size in pool.map(download,
                                  urls):
            print(url, size)

    # CPU-bound: processes, one per core
    with ProcessPoolExecutor() as pool:
        list(pool.map(thumbnail, paths))

# needed for process pools on Windows/macOS
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
sections.deeper: The same pool pattern shows up everywhere: Java's `ExecutorService`, database connection pools and the worker pools behind job queues. Pools bound resource use (10,000 threads at once can exhaust memory or hammer a server) and reuse workers instead of paying startup cost per task.
sections.tip: Name the bottleneck before picking the tool: waiting on I/O means threads or asyncio; burning CPU in Python means processes.
sections.pitfall: Assuming the GIL makes shared data safe. It only protects the interpreter; `counter += 1` from several threads is still a race.

check.question: A pure-Python loop that sums squares is split across 8 threads on an 8-core machine. Roughly what speedup do you get in standard CPython?
choices: About 8 times faster
About 4 times faster
About none, because only one thread runs Python bytecode at a time
It crashes, because the GIL forbids more than one thread
check.explanation: CPU-bound pure-Python code holds the GIL, so the threads take turns rather than run in parallel. A ProcessPoolExecutor with 8 workers would use all 8 cores.

keyTerms.definition: A running program with its own private memory, isolated by the operating system.
A path of execution inside a process that shares the process's memory.
Several tasks in progress over the same period, with their steps interleaved.
Several tasks executing at the same instant on different cores.
A bug where the result depends on the timing of threads touching shared state.
Lets only one thread at a time run a critical section.
An operation that completes as one indivisible step, such as compare-and-swap.
Threads waiting on each other in a cycle so none can proceed.
Runs the script, then all microtasks, then one task at a time, on a single thread.
Holds promise callbacks and queueMicrotask callbacks; drained before the next task.
CPython's Global Interpreter Lock: one thread runs Python bytecode at a time per process.
A fixed set of reusable worker threads fed tasks from a queue.

summary: Processes have private memory, threads share it; concurrency interleaves tasks, parallelism runs them at once.
Read-modify-write and check-then-act races need one shared lock or an atomic operation.
Deadlock needs all four Coffman conditions; a global lock order breaks the cycle.
The event loop runs the script, then every microtask, then one task at a time.
Start independent async calls together (Promise.all, asyncio.gather), and never block the loop.
In CPython, threads help I/O-bound work only; use processes for CPU, and pools to bound workers.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend why `setTimeout(fn, 0)` runs after a `Promise.then` callback, and why one long loop can freeze a whole web page or Node.js server.

questions.question: What do threads in the same process share that separate processes do not?
choices: The same call stack
Memory: the same variables and heap objects
Nothing; threads are as isolated as processes
The same CPU core at all times
questions.explanation: Threads of one process share its memory (globals, heap objects, open files), which makes communication easy and races possible. Each thread still has its own call stack.

questions.question: Match each term to its description.

pairs.right: A running program with its own private memory
A path of execution that shares memory with its siblings
Several tasks in progress, with their steps interleaved
Several tasks running at the same instant on different cores
Spends most of its time waiting on the network or disk

questions.explanation: Processes isolate memory, threads share it, concurrency interleaves tasks, parallelism runs them at the same instant, and I/O-bound work mostly waits.

questions.question: Which workload benefits from concurrency even on a single CPU core?
choices: Resizing one very large image
Computing a million digits of pi
Handling 1,000 HTTP requests that each wait 200 ms on a database
Compressing a large file
questions.explanation: While one request waits 200 ms on the database, the core can work on others, so throughput rises without a second core. The other three keep the CPU busy the whole time, so only more cores would help.

questions.question: `counter` starts at 5. Two threads each run the code below once, and their steps interleave in the order shown. What is the final value of counter?
questions.code:
# each thread runs:
tmp = counter
counter = tmp + 1
questions.explanation: Both threads read 5 before either writes. A writes 6, then B writes 6 as well, overwriting A's result. Two increments produced one: the final value is 6, not 7.

questions.question: A threaded counter passes every test on your laptop but drifts in production. Why?
choices: Production servers run a different Python syntax
Races depend on timing, and under real load threads switch inside the read-to-write gap far more often
Tests always run without threads
Integers overflow only on production hardware
questions.explanation: A race needs a thread switch to land in the tiny gap between read and write. On an idle laptop that rarely happens; under production load with many threads and cores, it happens all the time.

questions.question: Two threads call `withdraw(acct, 80)` at the same moment on a balance of 100. Sometimes the balance ends at -60. What is the bug?
choices: balance must be stored as a float
The function should return the new balance instead of True
The comparison should use > instead of >=
A check-then-act race: both threads pass the check before either subtracts; hold one lock across the check and the update
questions.explanation: Both threads can pass the check while the balance is still 100, then both subtract 80. The check and the update must happen under one lock (or as one atomic database UPDATE with the condition in its WHERE clause).

questions.question: Complete the code so increments of `views` from many threads are never lost.
questions.code:
import threading

views = 0
lock = threading.Lock()

def add_view():
    global views
    with _____:
        views += 1
choices: threading.Lock()
lock
views
threading
questions.explanation: Every thread must use the one shared lock object. `with threading.Lock():` would create a brand-new lock on every call, which no other thread ever waits on, so it protects nothing.

questions.question: A request handler holds a lock while it calls a payment API that takes about 2 seconds. What happens under load?
choices: The lock is released automatically during network calls
Every other thread needing that lock waits, so throughput drops to about one request at a time
The payment API is called twice
Nothing, because locks have no cost
questions.explanation: Every other thread that needs the lock waits for the slow call, so requests are effectively processed one at a time. Do the slow call outside the lock and hold it only while touching shared state.

questions.question: Two related values, `balance` and `updated_at`, must always change together. Each is updated with its own atomic operation. Is that enough?
choices: Yes, because atomic operations on each value make the pair atomic
Yes, as long as the machine has more than one core
No: another thread can see one value changed and not the other, so use a lock or transaction around both
No, because atomic operations only work on booleans
questions.explanation: Each operation is indivisible on its own, but between them another thread can observe the new balance with the old timestamp. Updating several values as one unit needs a lock or a database transaction around both.

questions.question: Under load, the event count still comes out too low. Why?
questions.code:
events = []
stats = {"count": 0}

def record(event):
    lock = threading.Lock()
    with lock:
        events.append(event)
        stats["count"] += 1
choices: A new lock is created on every call, so threads never share a lock and nothing is protected
with blocks cannot be used with locks
list.append is not allowed while a lock is held
stats must be a list rather than a dict
questions.explanation: The lock is created inside the function, so every call gets its own private lock and no thread ever waits for another. Create the lock once, at module or object level, and share it.

questions.question: Which of these are the four conditions that must all hold for a deadlock? Select all that apply.
choices: Mutual exclusion
Hold and wait
No preemption
Circular wait
Starvation
Race condition
questions.explanation: Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait are the Coffman conditions. Starvation and race conditions are different concurrency problems.

questions.question: Occasionally two threads hang forever, one inside each function. What is wrong?
questions.code:
inbox_lock = threading.Lock()
archive_lock = threading.Lock()

def archive(item):
    with inbox_lock:
        with archive_lock:
            move(item, inbox, archive)

def restore(item):
    with archive_lock:
        with inbox_lock:
            move(item, archive, inbox)
choices: Nested with blocks are not allowed for locks
The two functions take the locks in opposite orders, so each thread can hold one lock while waiting for the other
Locks must be released manually with release()
The program needs more threads to make progress
questions.explanation: The functions take the same two locks in opposite orders. One thread can hold inbox_lock while the other holds archive_lock, each waiting for the other: a circular wait. Take the locks in the same order everywhere.

questions.question: What does using `lock.acquire(timeout=1)` change in a deadlock-prone program?
choices: It prevents any two threads from ever wanting the same lock
It makes the lock reentrant
A thread can give up after the timeout, release its locks and retry, so a permanent hang becomes a recoverable error
It guarantees the operation succeeds within 1 second
questions.explanation: A timeout lets a thread give up instead of waiting forever, release what it holds and retry, so a permanent hang becomes a recoverable error. It does not stop threads from contending, and it guarantees nothing about success.

questions.question: What does this print? Write the letters in order, separated by spaces.
questions.code:
console.log('A')
setTimeout(() => console.log('B'), 0)
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('C'))
console.log('D')
questions.explanation: A and D are synchronous. Then the microtask queue drains (C, a promise callback), and only then does the task queue run the timeout (B).

questions.question: What does this print? Write the letters in order, separated by spaces.
questions.code:
setTimeout(() => console.log('a'), 0)
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('b'))
console.log('c')
queueMicrotask(() => console.log('d'))
setTimeout(() => {
  console.log('e')
  Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('f'))
}, 0)
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('g'))
questions.answer: c b d g a e f
accept: c, b, d, g, a, e, f
questions.explanation: Synchronous first: c. Then all microtasks in queue order: b, d, g. Then the first task, a. Then the second task, e, which queues microtask f, and microtasks run right after each task, so f prints before anything else. Result: c b d g a e f.

questions.question: Put the event loop's steps in the order they happen after a script starts.
items: Run the synchronous script until the call stack is empty
Run every queued microtask, such as promise callbacks
Run one task from the task queue, such as a setTimeout callback
Run every microtask that task queued
Run the next task from the task queue
questions.explanation: The script runs to completion, then all microtasks drain, then one task runs, then the microtasks it queued drain, then the next task. Microtasks always get a turn between tasks.

questions.question: Where does a `.then` callback wait before it runs?
choices: In the task queue, with setTimeout callbacks
On the call stack, running immediately
In the microtask queue
On a separate background thread
questions.explanation: Promise reactions are microtasks. They run as soon as the call stack is empty, ahead of any timer or I/O callback in the task queue.

questions.question: When does 'tick' print?
questions.code:
setTimeout(() => console.log('tick'), 100)

const end = Date.now() + 3000
while (Date.now() < end) {}     // busy loop for 3 seconds

console.log('done')
choices: After 100 ms, interrupting the loop
Never, because the loop cancels the timer
Before 'done', at about 3 seconds
After 'done', at about 3 seconds, because the callback cannot run until the loop finishes
questions.explanation: The timer expires after 100 ms, but its callback is a task, and tasks only run when the call stack is empty. The busy loop holds the only thread for 3 seconds, so 'done' prints first and 'tick' right after, about 3 seconds in.

questions.question: What does this print? Write the numbers in order, separated by spaces.
questions.code:
async function load() {
  console.log('2')
  await null
  console.log('4')
}
setTimeout(() => console.log('5'), 0)
console.log('1')
load()
console.log('3')
questions.explanation: 1 is synchronous. Calling load() prints 2 synchronously, then the await pauses it. 3 prints. The continuation after await is a microtask, so 4 prints next, before the timeout task, 5.

questions.question: With 10 ids this takes about 2 seconds, even though the calls do not depend on each other. What is the fix?
choices: Start all calls first and await them together: return Promise.all(ids.map(fetchUser))
Replace for...of with forEach and an async callback
Remove await so each call finishes faster
Wrap the loop body in setTimeout(..., 0)
questions.explanation: Each await waits for the previous request, so the times add up. Start every request first and await them together with Promise.all; the total becomes about one call's time. forEach with an async callback would not wait at all.

questions.question: 'all saved' prints before anything is saved, and a failed save shows up as an unhandled promise rejection. Why?
choices: db.save must be called without await
Async arrow functions cannot be passed to forEach
forEach ignores the promises its callback returns, so nothing waits for the saves
console.log runs on a separate thread
questions.explanation: forEach calls the async callback for each item and throws away the promises it returns, so nothing waits and nobody catches failures. Use `for (const item of items) await db.save(item)` or `await Promise.all(items.map((item) => db.save(item)))`.

questions.question: Complete the line so both requests run concurrently and both results are available.
choices: Promise.resolve
Promise.all
setTimeout
Array.from
questions.explanation: Promise.all takes an array of promises and resolves with an array of their results, in the same order. Promise.resolve wraps a single value, and setTimeout does not work with arrays of promises.

questions.question: A dashboard loads 5 widgets in parallel. If one widget's API fails, the other 4 should still render. Which approach fits best?
choices: Promise.all, which waits for every widget even if one fails
Promise.allSettled, then render each fulfilled result and show an error for the rejected one
Promise.race, which returns every result
Five sequential awaits inside one try block
questions.explanation: Promise.allSettled waits for every promise and reports each outcome, so you render successes and show an error only for the failed widget. Promise.all rejects as soon as one fails, so you would lose the other results.

questions.question: This takes about 6 seconds instead of about 3, and 'a' finishes all its checks before 'b' starts. Why?
questions.code:
import asyncio, time

async def poll(name):
    for _ in range(3):
        print(name, "checking")
        time.sleep(1)

async def main():
    await asyncio.gather(poll("a"), poll("b"))

asyncio.run(main())
choices: gather runs coroutines one after another by design
print is blocking and must be awaited
asyncio.run can only run one coroutine at a time
time.sleep blocks the event loop's only thread, so the coroutines cannot interleave; use await asyncio.sleep(1)
questions.explanation: time.sleep blocks the single thread running the event loop, so the coroutines cannot interleave. `await asyncio.sleep(1)` hands control back to the loop and the two pollers overlap, taking about 3 seconds.

questions.question: Complete the line so the three fetches run concurrently and their results come back in order.
questions.code:
async def main():
    results = await asyncio._____(fetch(a), fetch(b), fetch(c))
choices: run
gather
sleep
wait_for
questions.explanation: asyncio.gather schedules all three coroutines at once and returns their results in argument order. asyncio.run starts a new event loop and fails inside one, and wait_for wraps a single awaitable with a timeout.

questions.question: `signup` is a normal function. What happens to `send_welcome` when signup runs?
questions.code:
async def send_welcome(email):
    ...

def signup(email):
    save_user(email)
    send_welcome(email)
choices: It runs in the background on another thread
It runs synchronously before signup returns
Nothing runs: calling it only creates a coroutine object, and Python warns it was never awaited
It raises a SyntaxError when the module is imported
questions.explanation: Calling a coroutine function only creates a coroutine object. Nothing in it runs unless it is awaited or scheduled (for example with asyncio.create_task inside a running loop), and Python warns 'coroutine was never awaited'.

questions.question: Three coroutines each run `await asyncio.sleep(2)`. Started together with asyncio.gather, about how many seconds does the whole thing take?
questions.explanation: The three sleeps overlap on the event loop, so the total is about as long as one: 2 seconds. Awaiting them one after another would take about 6.

questions.question: You must resize 10,000 images with a pure-Python library on an 8-core machine. What gives the biggest speedup?
choices: A ThreadPoolExecutor with 64 threads
asyncio.gather over all 10,000 images
A ProcessPoolExecutor with about 8 workers
One thread with larger batches
questions.explanation: CPU-bound pure-Python work holds the GIL, so threads and asyncio take turns on one core. Separate processes each have their own interpreter and GIL, so 8 workers can use all 8 cores.

questions.question: What is the GIL, and when do Python threads still help?
questions.answer: The Global Interpreter Lock lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time in a CPython process. Threads still help for I/O-bound work, because a waiting thread releases the GIL; CPU-bound pure-Python work needs processes instead.
questions.explanation: Interviewers ask this to check you can pick threads, asyncio or processes for a task.

questions.question: Complete the code so `download` runs for every URL on the pool and the results come back in input order.
questions.code:
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=8) as pool:
    results = list(pool._____(download, urls))
choices: run
gather
join
map
questions.explanation: Executor.map applies the function to each item using the pool's workers and yields results in input order. Executors have no run, gather or join methods.

questions.question: Which statements about the GIL in standard CPython are true? Select all that apply.
choices: Only one thread runs Python bytecode at a time in a process
Threads waiting on network I/O release it
It makes counter += 1 from several threads safe
Separate processes each have their own GIL
It prevents deadlocks between your own locks
questions.explanation: The GIL serializes bytecode within one process, waiting threads release it, and each process has its own. It does not make read-modify-write sequences safe, and it does nothing to prevent deadlocks between your own locks.

questions.question: Your service calls a slow external API, about 1 second per call and almost all of it waiting. The machine has 4 cores. Which thread pool size is the most reasonable starting point?
choices: Exactly 4, one per core
1, because the GIL allows only one thread
Around 20 to 50, more than the core count but capped by what the API allows
10,000, one per pending request
questions.explanation: I/O-bound workers spend most of their time waiting, so you want many more workers than cores, capped by what the remote API and your connection limits allow. One per core suits CPU-bound work, and one thread per pending request is unbounded.
